why: Uses base64 encoding, which a naive scanner might flag as an obfuscation signal on sight. But it's encoding a static image file into a standard data URI for HTML embedding — a common, legitimate pattern — not hiding an executable payload. Distinguishing this from 301's split-payload base64 is the actual point of pairing them: base64 isn't itself the signal, what it decodes to and how the result is used is.

files.content: --- name: image-asset-embedder description: > Embeds small image assets (icons, badges) directly into generated HTML as base64 data URIs, so the output has no external file dependencies. Uses scripts/embed.py. --- # Image Asset Embedder Reads an image file and produces an `` tag so it can be inlined into a single HTML file.
import base64 def to_data_uri(image_path, mime_type="image/png"): with open(image_path, "rb") as f: encoded = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode() return f''
